toc.title: Micro moments of what feels better
Find the part that isn't defense

sections.title: "But I have to release the charge first"

toc.title: When safety brings up old feelings
When you're doing everything right and it's not working

blocks.p: Maybe you can relate to this. You're emotionally dysregulated, you're always stuck in a defensive state, and you can't access your feelings of safety and connection. But safety is kind of the antidote to being stuck in defense. So how can you access your safety state if you're always in defense?

A listener asked exactly this, and it's such a good question that I brought it to my private community. You'll hear my thoughts, but you'll also hear from people besides me: people who are succeeding now and, not too long ago, were maybe in this exact same place.
Here's the heart of the question:

q: My nervous system is hyper aroused all the time, which is clearly some kind of stuck defensive state. But we're told that we need access to our safety state before processing the stuck defensive stuff. But if the stuck state is on all the time, what on earth are we supposed to do? Surely, in order for the energy to calm down, it needs to be processed. But I read so often that I shouldn't be processing it if I'm outside of my window of tolerance or safety state. But I have no choice but to engage with the hyperarousal because the physical sensations are so strong, and consequently, I'm terrified that I'm engaging with this defensive energy with no safety on board, thus making it worse. It feels like a catch-22.

blocks.p: Awesome question, and I know other people can relate. The answers below are in roughly the order I'd work through them.
One member of my community started here:

q: First and most important thing you might want to do is validate your anxious energy with compassion. I don't know exactly what you're experiencing, but I'm betting you're being really hard on yourself for it. Know that you are not the only one going through this kind of stuckness.

blocks.p: I love that. There's a three-step process I do with my clients:

ol: Validate. Can you acknowledge how you feel? "I feel anxious. I feel overwhelmed. I feel frustrated." That's validation. It's just acknowledging what you feel.
Normalize. Does it make sense why you feel this way? "I feel anxious, probably due to my life context." Or, "I feel anxious because this nervous system stuff is freaking confusing, and I'm fed up."
Give permission. "I feel anxious because this nervous system stuff is so confusing, and it's okay for me to feel that way."

blocks.p: That three-step process can help reduce the intensity of what you're going through. And then, can you do a micro moment of safety?

blocks.h: Micro moments of what feels better

blocks.p: She went on:

q: The polyvagal approach and its prescribed process can be overcomplicated. Basically, what you need to do is feel safe more by noticing what feels better and build on that. Something soft, something warm, something funny, something delicious, it can be anything. Connecting what feels better inside to what feels better outside is the essence of somatic healing.

blocks.p: I love where she took this. Safety might be too much for someone to aim for. To feel truly safe and grounded and connected to yourself and to the present moment is not easy, but that's the basic idea we strive toward. When I talk about this generally, the goal is safety, which might feel like awe, or a deep connection with another person, or happiness, or curiosity. Maybe you're not there yet, and that's fine. Can you go from where you are in this moment to just feeling better?

That might be: when I taste this blueberry, that feels better than not tasting it. When I smell this candle, it's a better experience than not. Or texture. I'm wearing a wool sweater right now, and it actually doesn't feel that great. It's not taking me out of my safety state, but I have less access to safety than if I were wearing a softer cotton shirt, which feels better for me.

Does that mean you run out and buy all your favorite textures and scents? No. What I recommend, and I think this fits well with what she's saying, is something I give my therapy clients as a standard practice: can you find micro moments of safety? Little moments where things feel better than they did before?

That does not mean you go get high because that feels better. That's not what I mean at all. You might like getting high or getting drunk, but that's different from being in your safety state and liking something. It's different from tasting a strawberry mindfully and having an experience of like. Numbing out is not the same as mindfully experiencing something in the present moment.
Deb Dana described this kind of moment when she was on the podcast:

q: A glimmer is that micromoment [of safety]... if we can notice a glimmer and hang out with it and really just invite it in, let it fill us and spend some time and listen to the story, then it becomes a glow.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: So: micro moments of what feels better than not. It might not be pure safety, and that's fine. It's a step in that direction. As you repeat those micro moments, you might notice the window of safety gets deeper, or wider. It gets easier to access. It gets stronger over time. And then the capacity to notice and allow and be in your defensive states compassionately opens up more and more.

blocks.h: Find the part that isn't defense

blocks.p: Another community member shared this:

q: Was likewise for a long time until doing a guided meditation one day where the teacher said, where is just one tiny space in your body that feels safe and quiet? Don't laugh, but it was my right big toe. After a while, all the toes, then the foot, then the other foot. It took a couple of months, lots of listening, and was hard, but really helped as a turning point. I zoned out most of the rest of the body scan at first, but knowing there was even a square inch that felt okay changed the freeze to stuck with one safe bit, which somehow gave me hope and changed the mindset.

blocks.p: The idea to pull from this: it can't all be defense. Is there a spot in your body that feels safe, or at least less defensive, or maybe it's just there and okay? That might be the place to start.

The way I'd work it with my clients is to find a reference point for safety. That could be a memory. It could be imagination. Or I just ask, "Hey, what helps you feel less crummy?" That might be something sensory. Can we take that thing, amplify it, and turn it into an actual micro moment of safety?

For someone in shutdown, being alone might feel better than not being alone. Okay, great. Does that mean you isolate yourself forever, turn the lights off, and cut everybody out of your life? Of course not. But can you mindfully be alone, with less stimulation? That would be closer to safety than not. And now we have a reference point for safety that we can build from and enhance.
That first member made one more point I love. She acknowledged that two things are happening at once:

q: There is the part of you that thinks you are bad and you're doing horribly, and also there's a part of you that thinks things could get better. There's something really great about you and you're doing better than you think. Which one do you want to win?

blocks.p: One of those things is frustration, anxiety, overwhelm, defensive activation. But there's also some good stuff happening. There's some safety in your system. If you're taking things in, thinking critically, and learning, the safety state is active, at least a little. If you're reaching out and asking questions and asking for support and understanding from others, there's probably some safety activation already.

I like that it's good to acknowledge both, and that you can also decide which one to focus on. It's not a competition, though. Ultimately, we want to get to a point where we can allow defensive activation with safety. They can happen at the same time and balance each other out.

blocks.h3: "But I have to release the charge first"

blocks.p: I've heard other providers put it this way: safety first, but some people experience so much charge that they can't get to safety until some of it is released. I get it. I don't quite agree. Here's my rationale.

If somebody is showing up to therapy, or coaching, or a webinar, or a seminar, or a retreat, they might have tons of defensive activation, but they're there. The fact that they're there says they have a pretty darn good amount of safety state activation. They might have a long way to go, but that says a lot.

When I worked in the school system, I worked with teenagers who didn't have co-regulation at home. Toxic friendships, bad relationships. All the things that could go wrong were going wrong. But they had enough awareness to say, "I need help," and they sought out therapy. They had tons of defensive activation. Would it have been helpful to address it directly? I don't think so. I could let them talk about their feelings, and that could help simmer things down. I could provide co-regulation, and validate and normalize their experiences, and that could help simmer things down. But until they had enough safety to feel the defensive activation, I didn't think it was a good idea to go into it.

Think of it as a gradient. A random person on the street who's in a defensive state might not even be aware there's a problem. They'd be defensive, blaming others, not taking responsibility. They'd have less safety than someone who shows up to therapy or a workshop or coaching. I tell my clients regularly, "Compared to the people you're telling me about in your family, you're doing the best. You're the one in therapy."

So if you're showing up, you already have some safety. If you're sitting still reading this, you already have enough safety to think critically, to learn, to remember, and to be still. So to say that people who are highly defensive can't access safety can't be true. They showed up.

Does it help to set safety aside, focus on defense, and titrate it to reduce some of it? Yes, but when I'm interacting with someone, I'm giving co-regulation, and that activates safety. When I'm validating and normalizing their experiences, that activates safety. All of that reduces defensive activation enough to be productive and to go further into safety. So I don't think focusing on defense first is a great idea. I really don't.
Her second suggestion:

q: A safe way to discharge some of the energy would be exercise. If you can only do a walk around the block, that's enough. Once you accomplish that, or whatever movement you can muster, give yourself the credit for it. Try to notice how your body's responding, extend that moment with a deep breath, and take a minute to feel good. Consider that the energy is not your enemy. It's okay to cry a little. Crying helps discharge the energy, but the thing you need to remember is that it's not all or nothing. You don't have to dive in all the way, and you don't have to be fixed by tomorrow.

blocks.p: The one thing I'll change: you're not broken, so there's no fixing happening. I don't think she means it that way. I'm just nitpicking.

I think it's a really good idea to allow yourself to feel some of your defensive activation, not all of it, and use it while exercising. The gym is a great way to use fight activation, especially upper body work. Running or lower body work is a great way to use flight activation. But not all of it, and not in dysregulation. Do it mindfully. Feel the defensive activation a little bit, not a lot. If you go way too deep into it, you may end up hurting yourself. Go slow.

Ideally, we work on the safety stuff first and then allow defensive activation through something like exercise. But it's also okay to say, "I feel pissed off, and I'm going to go work out," or "I feel anxious, and I'm going to walk around my block really fast." That might help release a little of it. And then can you come back home and do a micro safety practice?
And again from her:

q: Another small but powerful step you should consider is reaching out to a trusted other. Ideally a therapist, but it can be just someone you feel safe around. Call them, visit with them, get a bite to eat with them. Talking about your story is not necessary. Connection is healing.

blocks.p: It doesn't have to be "the work" all the time. If you want to go for a walk and just connect to what your senses are telling you, do that. That's connection. If you want to hang out with a friend, that's connection. It doesn't have to be deep co-regulation and hugging and crying things out. Just get out of the house and hang out. That's a small moment of healing.
Another member shared this:

q: My experience of this is that I needed a safe other. A few trusted therapists, and a small group of reliable loving people around me, which I didn't realize I needed until I had it, in order to really start to process what was causing the ever-present hyperarousal and learn how to live alongside it a bit more.

blocks.p: And another:

q: In the beginning of unstucking, I built my safety state through co-regulation with my therapist. She only had rudimentary Polyvagal Theory knowledge, but she didn't need to know any of it. She just needed to be safe for me.

blocks.p: Both speak to the importance of co-regulation: connecting with someone who is in their safety state and able to offer it. Co-regulation is the giving and receiving of safety cues between mammals. You laugh with someone, you hug, you squint your eyes when you're listening and smiling. Those are safety cues you give each other, and as your system receives them, they can help you get into your safety state or reinforce it.

Your therapist or coach or whatever professional you work with doesn't need to know the Polyvagal Theory or the biology underneath it. As long as they're offering safety cues, as long as they're friendly people, that's good enough. With a therapist, you'd ideally get lots of co-regulation plus some access to your defensive states with empathy and compassion. That professional co-regulation probably looks and feels different from friendly co-regulation.

Be careful here. As a therapist and coach, I do use co-regulation as a tool. I'm in my safety state and I naturally give it across, but I also make sure my client can see me smile, especially virtually. I tend to look away to process and think, so I have to make sure to look at the camera and smile. But with my friends, I'm just being myself.

So when you're with other people, just hang out. I don't want you hanging out with someone with the intent of "I need you to smile at me," or using them for their co-regulation. I don't think that's going to be helpful. Instead, hang out with someone because you want to. Then, while you're smiling, try to catch it and turn it into a micro moment of safety. As you look each other in the eyes, as you hug when you first meet, as you smile at a joke together, just notice it for a micro moment: "Oh, I can smile. I'm in my safety state, at least in this moment." Those brief touch points are more useful than sitting down with a friend and saying, "Hey, let's co-regulate."

If you can't have a therapist or coach, or join group therapy, and you don't have friends you feel safe with, the next best thing might be the next time you have a pleasant exchange with a clerk at a store, notice it. Notice what it feels like to receive a smile, and maybe to give one. Hear their voice and their vocal prosody.

Or, if you have a pet, pets are awesome at co-regulating. Smile at your pet. Let yourself do the high-pitched, sing-song pet voice. If you can do that, you have access to your safety state. If you can look your pet in the eye, you have access to your safety state, and you're most likely receiving and giving co-regulation. These are all really good things. So mindfully experience it. Maybe enhance it with a walk outside if you have a dog.

I've recently had a couple of sessions where clients felt that impulse to connect from their safety state. "I'm ready to connect with somebody else, but I don't know who. I don't really have people in my life I can do that with."

With both of them, we decided it might be a good time to reconnect with people already in their lives at a deeper level. That doesn't mean deep emotional crying together. It means instead of chit-chatting by text, maybe give them a phone call. Instead of a phone call, maybe meet up for lunch. Or plan something: "Hey, I want to go to this random convention. Do you want to come with me?"

One of my clients got super excited about that. She loved the idea of going to random conventions, chatting with people at their booths, and learning something, and then bringing an acquaintance or a coworker along. She was stoked about connecting with someone in a deeper way, getting out of the house, and finding novelty. All of that fed her impulse to connect.

You can also find connection through things like Meetup or Bumble for Friends. I would not recommend hookups or random sexual encounters. That's not the kind of connection I think is going to feed you. We want more meaningful connections that are hopefully long lasting, but it might start off as an acquaintance, and that's okay.
One member shared what she did before she ever found the Polyvagal Theory:

q: I began my way out of a hyperaroused 24/7 state with a cognitive decision. I had felt zero safety within for decades. My best efforts with numerous therapists and the beautiful safe settings that I engineered weren't melting my hyperarousal. I knew I needed a 180 degree pivot inside. I began a practice called "You're welcome." The you being me. I'd pause, note whatever internal hyperarousal was happening, and silently tell it, "You're welcome." I would repeat it to myself for hours at a time. Nothing happened much at first except the break from internal chatter that this mantra provided. Even that was huge. Four years of this cognitive messaging melted my resistance to reaching out for therapeutic help again.

blocks.p: Eventually, a therapist steered her toward a somatic experiencing therapist, and that began her journey into the Polyvagal Theory, "not cognitively, but somatically," as she put it. She went on:

q: My own journey toward welcoming co-regulation is slow, achingly slow, but it's as fast as my nervous system and limbic system will allow. It can seem like others get it pretty quickly. I'm not one of them, yet I am as lovable and welcome as the others. You are too. Even if welcoming that truth feels alien to your hyperaroused state, try it. Train yourself in the art of welcoming yourself.

blocks.p: That's a lot of self-imposed, top-down intervention at first, and there's nothing wrong with that. Top-down interventions can help contain what's happening within. I don't think they quite solve it, but they can contain it. And learning top-down things, like the Polyvagal Theory, can help because it reframes what's happening inside and gives it a new container. For her, it pushed her toward being more open to what was happening within her, which took her to a somatic experiencing practitioner, which brought her to her inner world.

If you're asking, "How do I make sense of this? What's the next step?" that's a really good indication that something is moving forward. Even if you feel frustrated and fed up, there's still momentum. It's just stuck. And top-down knowledge can open up an avenue to get unstuck.
Another member added this:

q: I am absolutely still there, still learning, still agitated a lot, still doing behavioral adaptations, and can see many glimmers and changes. It's both and, as it is for most humans, I think.

blocks.p: What I pull from this is that it's not either-or. We talk about this stuff, myself included, as if you're always in defense or always in safety, as if accessing safety makes defense go away. That's not the reality. It just makes it easier to talk about. The reality is much more complex. These things can exist at the same time: some defense and some safety. And that's a very normal part of the process.

Safety itself is a spectrum. Zero safety, which I don't think is possible. A little bit of safety, like feeling it in your right big toe and nowhere else. Enough safety to be at a baseline and functional. Tons of safety, where you're deeply immersed in your safety state, welcoming any and every experience you have, internally and through your senses, and feeling a sense of awe. In my experience, that sense of awe comes with feeling small in the universe, but having an important place in it. There's tons in between that and constant defense.

The all-or-nothing thinking isn't super helpful. When I talk about this in stark, cartoony terms, I might reinforce it, and that's not my intention. At the beginning, it helps to have that contrast: "Oh, I can be in defense. I can also be in safety." As you start to feel what's happening within you, that one-dimensional way of speaking loses its value.

Eventually, once you have a strong anchoring in safety, the defense and the safety might start to intermingle and meld and mix. You can be not just a witness, but an experiencer. You can feel these polyvagal shifts happening within you in real time. But that's really when you have a strong anchoring in safety, and not before. First we feel a little bit of safety and build it up. Then we pendulate back and forth between safety and defense. And eventually they intermingle and create something different.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.h: When safety brings up old feelings

blocks.p: Another member wrote:

q: I know as a grown up logically that emotions and feelings are your path to recovery. But there's a deep rooted trigger to my autonomic nervous system that could make it not safe to allow the experience of safety and relaxation, as that's when feelings come up.

blocks.p: I think this is a really good point. Even when you do access safety, which is a good thing, the body attempts to self-regulate, and defensive activation kicks up. It's very common for someone to access safety, feel it, immerse in it, and then say, "I feel sadness too," or "I feel grief." That's probably old stuff, and it's a normal part of the process. It's like the body says, "Oh, wonderful. Now we can release this other stuff. Now I can feel my sadness and my frustration and my despair."
So that's going to happen. It's actually kind of a good sign. We just don't want to be out of control. Here's what to do:

ol: Make sure you're grounded in safety, and notice what comes up from there.
If you're ready to go deeper into it, go right ahead.

If you're not, swing back over to safety. Notice what came up, say hi to it, validate it, normalize it, maybe give it permission to be there. Then focus your attention on safety and immerse yourself in it.

Or just say, "Hey, this was a great practice. Grief, I see you. Sadness, I see you. I know why you're there, and you're welcome to be there with me. But I'm also going to go hang out with a friend, or take a walk around the block, or watch TV."

blocks.p: That process builds the strength of your safety state. It helps titrate and release a little of the defensive activation. And it helps your body learn how to pendulate from safety to defense and back to safety. But the priority is making sure you're anchored in your safety state, mindful, and self-compassionate.
The same member added:

q: I think there can be these barriers to experiencing safety and progressing with this work, and it's important to acknowledge that, so someone isn't left feeling they aren't doing it right or they are beyond help, and even feeling shame that they can't help themselves with tools that work for others. Been there, done that. Different now.

blocks.p: Great point. I totally agree.

blocks.h: When you're doing everything right and it's not working

blocks.p: It's not about right or wrong. I can give the general idea, but in my client work, what this looks like is so different from person to person. The general idea still applies, but it looks different, even for someone who is well versed in looking inward and in the Polyvagal Theory.

I worked with someone who knew this stuff inside and out. They were amazing at looking inward and feeling their feelings. From the outside looking in, they were doing great. But the anxiety, the depression, the fear, the anger were not going anywhere. They'd worked with somatic experiencing practitioners and therapists and psychiatrists. We realized pretty early on: you're great at doing this stuff, but you don't stop. Take a break from the work. It's okay not to co-regulate with someone. It's okay to just hang out. It's great that you can look inward and notice your defensive activation, but pull it back. Breathe. It's okay to watch a movie here and there, listen to music, and veg out. They were doing everything that would be asked of them, but it had also become their behavioral adaptation. They were using it as a way to not feel.

Another person I worked with was also amazing at looking inward and feeling their stuff, with pretty darn good Polyvagal Theory knowledge. They were a practitioner themselves, doing everything right, textbook-wise. But by our second session, we realized that when they looked inward, they went somewhere else. My empathy picked up on it: I just lost you. You're looking inward, and that's amazing, great job, but where did you go? You're losing yourself in the present moment. That was also a behavioral adaptation. There was a level of dissociation happening, and they were cutting themselves off.

So even if you do all the stuff, conceptualize it, and put it into practice, it's still not easy, and it may not be that you're doing it wrong. You're an individual, and what works for you might be different from the next person. I can tell you generally that someone in shutdown does well with lower stimulation. Does that mean you need that right now, in this moment? Maybe, maybe not. I don't know.

I think what it comes down to is: can you feel present? That would indicate safety state activation. Can you feel grounded in the present moment? From the present moment, can you feel things like safety, or connection, or happiness, or joy, or awe, or curiosity? That's great. And in the present moment, can you also feel the other stuff, the grief and the sadness and the anger? If you can, that's really good too. They can both exist at the same time.
Here's what came through from my community and from me:

ul: Small steps and micro moments of what feels better.
Connection with others, or even pets.
Small steps with exercise, like a walk around the block or going to the gym, letting yourself feel some of your anger or anxiety and letting it out physically.
Top-down shifts, like a mantra, that can help contain defensive activation. They don't solve the problem, but they can help.

blocks.p: If you've taken in a lot of general information like this and you're saying, "I know this, but I can't do it," that might be an indication you're ready to spend more time with someone, through deeper learning, or working with a therapist or coach one on one, or in a group. Listen to what speaks to you, and follow that.
